newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela promises Taiwan all, except diplomatic ties.
newsitem.headline: Mandela promises Taiwan all, except diplomatic ties.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Wednesday he would stick by his "agonising" decision last week to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but promised to maintain ties in all but name.

"We are going to maintain relations on the highest level, short of diplomatic relations," he told a news conference after talks with Taiwanese Foreign Minister John Chang which failed to reverse the decision to switch diplomatic ties from Taiwan to China.
A bilateral committee is to be set up to work out the details -- such as whether a consular office might remain.
Mandela would not comment on how he would deal with any possible objections from Beijing to such close links.
He said he was encouraged by remarks by business leaders in Taipei that the end of formal relations would not affect major Taiwanese investments in South Africa.
Relations with Beijing will improve prospects for better trade with one of the world's biggest economies, though at the moment Taiwanese investments in South Africa are greater.

Chang, sent to South Africa to ask about the diplomatic setback which Taiwan said it had had no warning of, told the same news conference he was confident Pretoria and Taipei could come to an arrangement in the interests of both countries.
"The people and the government of (the Republic of) China understand the reasons behind the very, very difficult and painful decision President Mandela has made," he added.

Mandela, who said in August it would be immoral for him to dump Taipei in order to establish diplomatic links with China, made a sudden u-turn last week and said Pretoria would switch recognition to Beijing by the end of 1997.

A regional superpower keen to play a bigger global role now since political isolation was swept away with apartheid, South Africa yielded to China's insistence it would not recognise any country that allowed Taiwan an embassy.
"At the end of next year we will sever diplomatic relations with Taiwan, the Republic of China," Mandela said at his offices in Pretoria's Union Buildings, making clear the decision was final.

"I have agonised over this decision because I know precisely what it will mean to the government and people of that country, but there comes a time when a man must, in the interest of his own country, take a decision even if it hurts."

Analysts said the one-year delay until ties end was a vain attempt by Mandela to soften the blow of derecognition for a country which gave his African National Congress strong support in the run-up the the 1994 elections that ended white rule.
South Africa was Taiwan's biggest diplomatic ally, its defection to Beijing leaves Taipei with diplomatic relations with just 29 nations, most of them small and poor which receive Taiwanese aid.
Communists took power in mainland China in 1949 after a civil war that left the former Nationalist government in control only of the island of Taiwan.

Beijing insists Taiwan must come under its control and has waged a successful diplomatic war to isolate Taipei, which lost China's seat at the United Nations in the early 1970s when Washington also switched recognition to Beijing.
South Africa's relations with Taiwan date back to the apartheid era when both were diplomatic pariahs.
